title: continuous-batching-scheduler-draft
content:
Purpose:
This is an internal draft describing design alternatives and tradeoffs for a continuous batching scheduler in the serving runtime. Focus: token-level vs request-level scheduling and fairness policies that interact with KV cache behavior and kernel selection.

Background and motivation:
- Continuous batching is central to achieving high GPU utilization and low per-token cost while meeting latency SLOs.
- Our serving runtime already supports dynamic batching by grouping requests up to a batch size threshold, but we need to formalize a scheduler that operates continuously at token granularity to better utilize KV caching and reduce wasted compute from padding.
- Key constraints: heterogeneous sequence lengths, multiple tenant priorities, kernel-level performance sweet spots (e.g., matrix sizes that map to fast kernels), and KV cache locality across requests.

Goals:
- Maximize throughput (tokens/sec) without breaking latency SLOs for prioritized classes.
- Minimize extra token work due to padding and inefficient kernel selection.
- Provide configurable fairness primitives (per-request fairness, per-token fairness, weighted priorities).
- Ensure predictable interaction with KV cache: avoid excessive cache churn and wasted KV copies.

Problem statement and tradeoffs:
- Request-level batching (classic): group whole requests. Simpler bookkeeping. Good when requests are similar length and arrive in bursts. But suffers from padding overhead when sequence lengths vary and from suboptimal kernel sizes (e.g., small micro-batches).
- Token-level batching (continuous): schedule tokens across requests as they arrive, forming batches of tokens to compute the next transformer step. Pros: reduced padding, better opportunity to fill GPU kernels, more consistent hardware utilization. Cons: more complex state management, preemption/partial completion, fairness pitfalls (starvation or head-of-line blocking), KV cache complexity because interleaving requests may need separate KV states kept warm.

Definitions and primitives used below:
- active-request: a request in the pipeline that has produced some initial tokens and expects subsequent tokens (chat-style or streaming generation).
- token-step: one autoregressive step for a particular active-request (taking previous KV cache + new input tokens => new tokens + KV updates).
- batch-window: a small time slice or collector period where tokens are aggregated to form a kernel invocation. Configurable (e.g., 0.5ms–5ms).
- kernel-group: classification of sequences by length/shape that maps to a particular kernel or kernel configuration.

Scheduler design options:
1) Epochal request-level scheduler (baseline)
   - Collect requests for up to T ms or until max_batch reached.
   - Build batch by padding sequences to max length in batch.
   - Run kernel; update KV caches.
   - Simple fairness: FIFO, optional weight per-customer.
   - Interaction with KV cache: good per-request locality, contiguous KV update.
   - When to use: high SLOs for short bursty traffic and homogeneous seq lengths.

2) Continuous token-level scheduler (fine-grained)
   - Maintain a queue of active-requests; for each request track remaining tokens to generate and its KV state.
   - Continuously form token batches every X ms or as tokens accumulate to target_token_batch_size.
   - Optionally coalesce tokens from multiple requests to match kernel-group shapes (pad to small multiples instead of full seq pad).
   - Preemption: a request may be partially served (n tokens) and re-queued.
   - Fairness is enforced at token granularity (explained below).

3) Hybrid scheduler (adaptive)
   - Default to token-level continuous scheduling when active-concurrency is high and seq length variance is large.
   - Fall back to request-level epochs when incoming requests are homogenous or latency-critical single requests exist.
   - Use metrics to switch modes: padding overhead, average batch utilization, observed GPU kernel throughput.

Fairness policies (requirements):
- Per-request fairness: each request should make forward progress proportional to its weight; useful for fairness across customers and to enforce per-request latency limits.
- Per-token fairness: fairness is measured in tokens scheduled; long requests are proportionally more served. This tends to favor large-compute requests, but yields better overall throughput fairness for token-based billing.
- Deadline-aware fairness: requests can include a soft deadline/latency budget; scheduler prioritizes meeting deadlines.

Implementation ideas for fairness in token-level scheduler:
A) Credit-based allocator (recommended prototype)
   - Each request r has a weight w_r. Maintain credits C_r initially proportional to w_r.
   - When scheduler selects k tokens from r for a batch, decrement C_r by k.
   - Periodically refill credits at a rate proportional to w_r.
   - When a request is out of credits, deprioritize until next refill.
   - Benefits: smooth proportional fairness, simple to reason about, can be extended with deadline boosts.

B) Weighted round-robin at token granularity
   - Maintain per-queue pointers, select one token from each queue in round; repeat according to weights.
   - Easier to implement but might be inefficient for kernel packing (many tiny toggles).

C) Max-wait / starvation prevention
   - Track waiting time; if a request exceeds max_wait, temporarily boost weight or allocate an immediate mini-batch.

KV cache considerations:
- Each active-request holds its own KV state; token-level scheduling frequently switches between KV contexts. That implies:
   - GPU memory pressure: we must cap the number of concurrent active-request states resident in GPU memory.
   - Warm-up cost: moving KV to GPU or reattaching a context has latency. Favor keeping hot requests resident.
- Strategies:
   1) Resident set management: LRU-like retention of hot KV states, pinning for high-weight requests.
   2) KV shards per GPU: group active-requests so that contiguous entries enable efficient memory access patterns.
   3) Prefetching: when a request is likely to be scheduled soon (credit high, deadline close), ensure its KV is resident.
   4) Mini-batching KV ops: coalesce KV writes from multiple requests to amortize memory stalls.

Kernel selection and batch shaping:
- Kernel performance depends strongly on micro-batch size and sequence lengths. The scheduler should be kernel-aware:
   - Maintain recent kernel_nanos for (kernel-group, batch-size) pairs.
   - Prefer forming batches that land on efficient kernel pivot points (e.g., multiples that match cuBLAS/cutlass tiling).
   - Allow slight padding at token-level to reach a better kernel size if that reduces overall compute time.

Pseudocode (high-level):
- data structures:
  active_requests = priority queue keyed by next_allowed_time / credits / deadline
  token_collector = list
  timer every batch_window_ms:
    while token_collector.size < target_tokens and active_requests not empty:
      r = pop(active_requests)
      n = allocate_tokens(r, remaining_token_budget)
      append (r, n) to token_collector
    if token_collector not empty:
      grouped = group_by_kernel_group(token_collector) // heuristic; try to form homogeneous groups
      for g in grouped: run_kernel(g) // issue GPU work
      update credits, deadlines, KV states
      reinsert incomplete requests into active_requests

Allocation policy notes:
- allocate_tokens should consider: remaining seq length, credits, per-request max_tokens_per_turn, kernel packing benefit.
- configurable knobs: target_tokens_per_kernel, max_tokens_per_request_per_batch, max_active_resident_kv_contexts.

Metrics to evaluate and track:
- tokens/sec, avg latency (p50/p90/p99) per-weight-class, padding_tokens/(total_tokens), kernel utilization (GPU occupancy), KV context swaps/sec, number of active-resident-KV-contexts, fairness gap (e.g., deviation from ideal proportional progress).

Experiments to run (suggested):
1) Synthetic workload: mix of short (<=16 tokens) and long (>=512 tokens) sequences with Poisson arrivals. Compare request-level vs token-level vs hybrid on throughput and p99 latencies.
2) Kernel pivot experiment: compare policy that allows +X tokens padding to reach a known kernel sweet spot vs strict minimal padding.
3) KV resident set sizing: vary max resident contexts and measure effect on average latency and throughput.
4) Fairness policies: implement credit-based and RR; measure per-tenant fairness metrics and throughput.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Starvation: enforce max_wait and boost policies, or hard guarantees for premium SLAs.
- KV memory OOM: cap active resident contexts, fall back to request-level batching for cold requests (schedule them less frequently but in larger contiguous batches).
- Kernel misprediction: degrade gracefully by switching grouping heuristics if recent kernel timings deviate.

Open questions / design decisions to take:
- Default policy for free-tier vs paid tenants: per-token fairness or per-request fairness? Recommendation: bill-by-token customers get token-weighted fairness; premium customers can request weight boosts or latency SLO pins.
- How aggressive should padding-for-kernel be? Need cost model: extra tokens * token_cost vs decreased kernel time.
- How to surface KV residency metrics to product teams for debugging and cost allocation?

Next steps / TODOs:
- Prototype credit-based continuous scheduler in a test harness. Implement basic KV resident set with simple pin/LRU policy.
- Run synthetic workload experiments and capture metrics listed above.
- Integrate kernel-timing telemetry into scheduler decision path.
- Draft API extensions: per-request weight, optional deadline/latency budget, max_tokens_per_turn.
- Review security impacts for multi-tenant KV residency (isolation expectations).

Notes-to-self / implementation hints (informal):
- Keep batch_window_ms small (1-3ms) for low-latency interactive use; increase for throughput mode.
- Avoid token preemption inside a KV step (do not slice a single transformer block execution), preemption happens between token-steps only.
- For beam search / sampling, ensure replica tokens from same request prefer to be scheduled together to reduce branching overhead.

References and related artifacts:
- Confluence SCHED-987 (scheduling spec overview)
- Benchmark data: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/812
- Previous implementation notes in jira SCHED-1212.

End of draft.
